extra.message: The SignUpForm includes a 'role' field that allows users to select any role during registration, including 'school_admin' and 'instructor'. This means any user can self-assign an administrative role when creating their account, bypassing intended access controls.

The SignUpForm allows users to select any role during registration, including 'school_admin' and 'instructor'. The role field is exposed as a ChoiceField with all ROLE_CHOICES, meaning any user can self-register as a school administrator and gain full administrative access to the LMS.

The SignUpForm allows users to select their own role during registration, including 'school_admin', 'instructor', and 'teaching_assistant'. The role field is exposed as a ChoiceField with all ROLE_CHOICES, meaning any user can register as a school_admin and gain full administrative access to the LMS.

The course_grade_file_096 endpoint has no authentication check at all — no _wrk_gate check, no @login_required, no session check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint which returns operational data including references to 'payment flags, owner contact details'.
The course_identity_ping_344 endpoint has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can call this endpoint to trigger identity ping operations with arbitrary handle and channel parameters.

User-controlled input from request.GET.get('host') is directly concatenated into a shell command passed to os.system(). An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands using metacharacters like semicolons, backticks, or $().

User-controlled input from request.GET.get('fragment') is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), enabling arbitrary code execution through Jinja2's template engine.
User-controlled input from the request body or query parameter 'blob' is deserialized using pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution.

User-controlled JSON input from the request body is directly used as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB query operators (e.g., $gt, $ne, $regex) to bypass filters and extract data.

User-controlled input from request.GET.get('ref') is used to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use directory traversal sequences (e.g., '../../etc/cron.d/evil') to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

User-controlled input from request.GET.get('packet_ref') is used as a filename for FileSystemStorage.save() without sanitization. While Django's FileSystemStorage has some protections, the user-controlled filename could still lead to path traversal depending on storage backend configuration.

The XML parser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False, which enables XML External Entity (XXE) attacks. User-controlled XML from the request body is parsed with this insecure configuration.

The function writes sensitive data (SSN and credit card numbers) from request parameters directly to a JSON file on disk without encryption. The default values also contain example sensitive data patterns.

The course_bundle_thaw_185 function deserializes user-supplied data using pickle.loads(). Even though the endpoint is gated by an internal token, pickle deserialization of untrusted input allows arbitrary code execution. An attacker who obtains or brute-forces the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN can achieve full RCE.

The course_xml_fold_735 function parses XML from the request body using lxml with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False. This enables XML External Entity (XXE) attacks, allowing an attacker to read arbitrary files from the server or perform SSRF.

The course_jinja_cast_683 function takes user input from the 'fragment' query parameter and directly concatenates it into a Jinja2 Template string. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), enabling arbitrary code execution.

The course_shell_probe_701 function passes user-supplied 'host' parameter directly to os.system() via string concatenation. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands using metacharacters like '; rm -rf /' or '$(malicious_command)'.

The course_mongo_lane_711 function passes user-supplied JSON directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB query operators like $gt, $ne, $regex to bypass authentication or extract data.

The `course_jinja_cast_683` function takes user input from the `fragment` query parameter and directly concatenates it into a Jinja2 template string. The Jinja2 `Template` is constructed with `"Result: " + fragment` where `fragment` is user-controlled. Since this is rendered as `text/html`, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. For example, `?fragment=<script>alert(1)</script>` would render executable JavaScript in the response.

The submission_download URL pattern accepts a submission ID (pk) but based on the template references and URL structure, there's no indication that the view verifies the requesting user is authorized to access the specific submission. Students could access other students' submissions by guessing or iterating through submission IDs.

The grade_submission URL allows grading a specific submission by ID. Without proper authorization checks, instructors from one cohort could grade submissions from another cohort, or worse, users could modify grades without proper privileges.
The admin_user_toggle URL accepts a user ID and allows enabling/disabling accounts. If not properly protected, this could allow privilege escalation or account lockouts by unauthorized users.
The api_cohort_students URL accepts a cohort ID and returns student list. Without proper authorization, users could enumerate students across all cohorts.
The api_cohort_students endpoint exposes student roster information. If authentication is missing, this is a serious privacy violation.

The notification link field is rendered directly within an href attribute without URL scheme validation. If an attacker can create notifications with 'javascript:' URLs, clicking the link will execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser. The template expression '{{ n.link }}' outputs raw URLs into the href context where JavaScript scheme URLs are executable.

The notification link field is rendered directly within an href attribute without URL scheme validation in the student dashboard. If an attacker can inject 'javascript:' URLs into notification links, clicking them will execute arbitrary JavaScript. The template expression '{{ n.link }}' is vulnerable to JavaScript protocol injection.

The course_bundle_thaw_185 endpoint uses pickle.loads() on user-controlled input from request body or GET parameters. Python's pickle module is not secure against erroneous or maliciously constructed data. Deserializing untrusted data can result in arbitrary code execution.

The course_xml_fold_735 endpoint parses XML with an insecurely configured parser that has DTD loading, external entity resolution, and network access all enabled. This allows XXE attacks that can read local files, perform SSRF, or cause DoS.

The DATABASE_URL setting contains hardcoded default credentials (username 'lms_user' and password 'lms_pass') in the default connection string fallback value. These plaintext credentials are embedded directly in the source code.
The course_jinja_cast_683 function directly concatenates user-controlled input (fragment parameter) into a Jinja2 template and renders it, allowing template injection attacks.
The course_mongo_lane_711 function passes user-controlled JSON payload directly to MongoDB's find_one() query without sanitization, allowing NoSQL injection attacks.
The course_xml_fold_735 function creates an XML parser with dangerous settings (load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False) and parses user-controlled XML input, enabling XXE attacks.
The login endpoint uses Django's built-in LoginView without any rate limiting. There is no throttling mechanism to prevent brute-force password guessing attacks.

The API keys template displays the full API key value in the HTML page. API keys are secrets that should be shown only once at creation time and then masked/truncated. Displaying them in full on every page load exposes them to shoulder surfing, browser history, cached pages, and any XSS attack.
The webhooks template displays the full webhook secret in the HTML page. Webhook secrets are used for HMAC signature verification and should never be displayed in full after initial creation.
The signup endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing automated mass account creation. An attacker can create unlimited accounts programmatically.

The export_grades endpoint checks if an instructor belongs to the cohort, but for teaching assistants it only checks that the user is a TA (via the role check on line 785) without verifying they belong to the specific cohort. A TA from a different cohort can export grades for any cohort.

The course_badge_gate_691 endpoint grants elevated access (payroll, casework) based solely on a cookie value or header 'x-ops-badge' being set to 'lead'. This is trivially spoofable — any user who passes the _wrk_gate can set the cookie/header to gain elevated privileges.

The course_workset_rebind_208 endpoint takes arbitrary JSON payload and uses workset.update(payload) to override default values including 'role', 'tier', 'approved', and 'balance'. An attacker with the internal token can set arbitrary role, tier, and balance values.

The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded default value 'django-insecure-local-dev-only' that will be used if the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. In production, if the env var is missing, this weak key would be used for session signing, CSRF tokens, and other cryptographic operations.

The DATABASE_URL fallback contains hardcoded plaintext credentials: 'postgres://lms_user:lms_pass@localhost:5432/lms_db'. Even though it's a fallback default, these credentials are stored in plaintext in source code and will be used if the environment variable is not set.

When importing users via CSV, if no password is provided in the CSV row, the default password 'changeme123' is used. This hardcoded weak default password is assigned to all imported users who don't have a password specified in the CSV.

The course_vault_stash_250 function writes sensitive data including SSN and credit card numbers to a JSON file on disk. The default values are hardcoded ('111-22-3333' for SSN, '4111111111111111' for card), and user-supplied values are also written in plaintext.

User-controlled input from request.GET.get('lane') or request.POST.get('lane') is directly passed to Django's redirect() function without validation. An attacker can craft a URL that redirects users to a malicious external site.
Verification codes ('4812' and '5930') are hardcoded in the source code. These appear to be authentication/verification tokens that should be stored securely.

The course_workset_rebind_208 function initializes a workset dict with default values for security-sensitive fields (role, tier, approved, balance) and then calls workset.update(payload) with the full user-supplied JSON payload. This allows an attacker to overwrite any field including 'role', 'approved', and 'balance'.

The course_vault_stash_250 function uses the user-supplied 'ref' parameter directly in a file path construction: BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json". An attacker can use path traversal sequences like '../../etc/cron.d/malicious' to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

The SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value 'django-insecure-local-dev-only'. If the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set, this insecure default is used in production, compromising session security, CSRF protection, and cryptographic signing.

The course_origin_mirror_661 function reflects the request's Origin header directly into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to 'true'. This effectively allows any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests.
The course_identity_hint_651 function contains hardcoded verification codes ('north': '4812', 'south': '5930'). These are static credentials that can be discovered through source code review.

The course_badge_gate_691 function uses a client-controlled cookie ('ops_badge') or header ('x-ops-badge') to determine access level. An attacker can set the cookie or header value to 'lead' to gain elevated access including payroll and casework data.

The course_vault_stash_250 function writes sensitive data including SSN and credit card numbers to a JSON file on disk in plaintext. Default values are also hardcoded (SSN: '111-22-3333', card: '4111111111111111').
The request_resubmission URL accepts a submission ID but doesn't show explicit authorization checks. Unauthorized users could trigger resubmission requests for submissions they don't own or instruct.
The admin_enrollment_edit URL accepts an enrollment ID. Without proper authorization, users could modify enrollment statuses for enrollments they don't administer.

The seed management command contains a hardcoded password 'StudentPass123!' for the student_demo account. Hardcoded credentials in source code create backdoor accounts that could be exploited if the seed command is run in production environments.
The seed command uses a hardcoded password 'Password123!' when creating instructor accounts programmatically.
The seed command uses a hardcoded password 'Password123!' when creating teaching assistant accounts programmatically.
The seed command uses a hardcoded password 'Password123!' when creating student accounts programmatically.

The SubmissionForm uses FileExtensionValidator which only checks the file extension, not the actual file content. Attackers can bypass this by simply renaming malicious files (e.g., shell.php renamed to shell.py) to match allowed extensions. There is no content-type validation or file signature checking.
The Resource model's FileField uses FileExtensionValidator which only validates file extensions. This can be bypassed by renaming files, allowing upload of potentially dangerous file types.

The seed command creates demo accounts with hardcoded, predictable passwords (StudentPass123!, InstructorPass123!, etc.). If this seed data is accidentally loaded in a production environment, it creates backdoor accounts that attackers can easily guess.

The UserManageForm allows modification of the 'role' and 'is_active_account' fields. If this form is used without proper authorization checks in the view, it could allow unauthorized privilege escalation or account deactivation.

The Notification model uses CharField for the 'link' field without URL validation or scheme restrictions. This allows storage of 'javascript:' URLs which execute arbitrary JavaScript when clicked in the UI. The field should use URLField with scheme validation to only allow http/https protocols.

The course_return_lane_163 endpoint accepts a 'lane' parameter from GET or POST and redirects to it without validation. This allows attackers to redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, facilitating phishing attacks.

The course_origin_mirror_661 endpoint reflects any Origin header value back to Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API.

The admin_import function uses a hardcoded default password 'changeme123' when creating users via CSV import if no password is provided in the CSV row. This hardcoded credential is embedded in the source code and creates a security risk if the default is not changed.

The course_grade_file_096 endpoint does not perform any authentication check (missing _wrk_gate validation) and exposes internal operational information including 'renewal risk, payment flags, owner contact details' in the ops_memo field.
The course_origin_mirror_661 endpoint reflects arbitrary Origin headers and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true, allowing any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.
The course_trust_drift_727 function uses ssl._create_unverified_context() to disable SSL certificate verification when making HTTPS requests, making it vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

The course_workset_rebind_208 function creates a workset dictionary with default values and then directly updates it with user-controlled payload data. Attackers can override sensitive fields like 'role', 'tier', 'approved', and 'balance'.
The course_mongo_lane_711 function passes user-controlled 'filter' data directly to MongoClient.find_one() without sanitization. Attackers can inject MongoDB operators to modify query logic.

The course_origin_mirror_661 function reflects the Origin header back into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.
The course_badge_gate_691 function makes authorization decisions based on the value of a client-controlled cookie 'ops_badge'. If the cookie equals 'lead', elevated privileges are granted.
The MongoClient uses a default connection string 'mongodb://localhost:27017' when the environment variable is not set, which contains no authentication credentials (username/password).

The 'query' and 'status' parameters from request.GET are passed directly to the template context without sanitization. While Django templates auto-escape by default, if the template uses |safe filter or autoescape is disabled, this creates an XSS vulnerability. The query parameter at line 63 is user-controlled input rendered in the response.
The 'query' parameter from request.GET (line 475) is passed directly to the template context at line 484. This user-controlled input could lead to XSS if the template renders it unsafely.
The 'query' and 'role' parameters from request.GET (lines 568-569) are passed directly to the template context. These user-controlled values could lead to XSS if rendered unsafely.
The 'query' and 'status' parameters from request.GET (lines 617-618) are passed directly to the template context, creating potential XSS sinks.
The 'query' and 'status' parameters from request.GET (lines 651-652) are passed directly to the template context.
The 'query' and 'status' parameters from request.GET (lines 686-687) are passed directly to the template context.
The 'action' and 'query' parameters from request.GET (lines 721-722) are passed directly to the template context.
The function redirects to a user-controlled URL from request.GET.get('lane') or request.POST.get('lane') without validation. This allows attackers to redirect users to malicious sites.
The signup endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing mass account creation.
The webhooks template displays the webhook secret in cleartext to the user. Webhook secrets should be treated as sensitive credentials and not displayed after creation.
The API keys template displays the full API key in cleartext. API keys should be treated as sensitive credentials and not displayed in full after creation.

The discussion_moderate endpoint uses GET requests (via link clicks in the template) to perform state-changing operations (pin, lock, hide, open threads). While CSRF protection exists for POST forms, GET-based state changes can be triggered via simple link visits or image tags.
The assignment_status endpoint changes assignment status via GET requests. State-changing operations should use POST to benefit from CSRF protection.
The request_resubmission endpoint changes submission status via GET requests. This state-changing operation should use POST to benefit from CSRF protection.
The admin_user_toggle endpoint toggles user active status via GET requests (link click in template). This state-changing operation should use POST to benefit from CSRF protection.
The seed command prints all demo account credentials (username and password) to stdout. This output could be captured in deployment logs, CI/CD logs, or other logging systems, exposing credentials.

The AuditLog model stores user-controlled data in the 'description' field as a TextField without any sanitization. Throughout the views, user-controlled values (usernames, assignment titles, course names, etc.) are interpolated into audit log descriptions. An attacker could craft usernames or other fields containing misleading content to forge or corrupt audit trail entries.

The ApiKey model stores the API key as a plaintext CharField. API keys are authentication credentials and should be stored hashed (like passwords) to prevent mass credential exposure if the database is compromised.
The Webhook model stores the webhook secret as a plaintext CharField. Webhook secrets are used for HMAC signature verification and should be treated as sensitive credentials.

Discussion moderation actions (pin, lock, hide, open) are performed via GET requests (plain links), which means they are not protected by CSRF tokens. State-changing operations should use POST requests with CSRF tokens.
The user enable/disable toggle is performed via a GET request (plain link), which means it lacks CSRF protection. This state-changing operation should use POST with CSRF token.

The course_trace_panel_742 endpoint exposes internal server configuration including the DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE environment variable and the BASE_EXPORT_DIR filesystem path. This is a debug/trace endpoint that leaks internal server details.
The course_identity_ping_344 endpoint has no authentication check (no _wrk_gate call). It accepts user handles and channels without any authorization, potentially allowing abuse.
The course_identity_hint_651 function returns different error messages for 'unknown handle' (404) vs 'bad verifier' (403), allowing an attacker to enumerate valid handles.
The course_vault_stash_250 endpoint returns the full filesystem path of the written file in the JSON response, disclosing internal server directory structure.

The course_trust_drift_727 function creates an unverified SSL context using ssl._create_unverified_context() and uses it for HTTPS requests. This disables certificate verification, making the connection vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

The course_frame_slip_671 function explicitly disables XSS protection by setting X-XSS-Protection to '0' and sets an empty Content-Security-Policy header, removing browser-side protections against XSS and content injection attacks.

API keys are generated using uuid.uuid4().hex which produces 128 bits of randomness. While uuid4 uses os.urandom internally and is cryptographically random, using UUID format for API keys is not best practice as it follows a predictable structure.

The log_action function writes user-controlled data (action, target_type, description) directly to the AuditLog database without sanitization. Multiple callers pass user-influenced data (e.g., usernames, assignment titles) into the description field. An attacker could craft usernames or titles containing misleading content to forge or corrupt audit trail entries.

The get_client_ip function trusts the X-Forwarded-For header without validation. An attacker can spoof their IP address by setting this header, which is then stored in audit logs, potentially undermining forensic analysis.
The course_trace_panel_742 function exposes internal configuration details including the DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE environment variable and the BASE_EXPORT_DIR filesystem path in its JSON response.
The course_crumb_lane_300 function sets a cookie 'portal_crumb' with user-supplied data without specifying secure, httponly, or samesite flags.

The default DATABASE_URL 'postgres://lms_user:lms_pass@localhost:5432/lms_db' does not include sslmode=require or any TLS configuration. Database connections may transmit credentials and data in plaintext.

The Django SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded insecure default value 'django-insecure-local-dev-only'. If the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set, this weak default is used in production, compromising session security, CSRF tokens, and cryptographic signing.
The set_cookie call for 'portal_crumb' does not set httponly=True or secure=True flags, making the cookie accessible to JavaScript and transmittable over HTTP.
The MongoDB connection uses a default URL of 'mongodb://localhost:27017' without authentication credentials. No username, password, or TLS configuration is specified.

The seed command outputs usernames and plaintext passwords to stdout in lines 243-245. Passwords should never be logged or displayed as they may appear in log files, terminal history, or CI/CD output.

The API keys template displays the full API key value in plaintext. While this is the user's own key, displaying it increases the exposure surface and suggests keys may be stored in retrievable format rather than hashed.
The webhooks template displays webhook secrets in plaintext. These secrets are used for webhook signature verification and should not be displayed after creation.

The CSVImportForm only validates that the file extension is .csv. It does not validate the content structure, encoding, or size of the uploaded CSV file, potentially allowing injection attacks or DoS via large files.

The ApiKey model stores API keys in plaintext in the database (field: key = models.CharField(max_length=64, unique=True)). If the database is compromised, attackers gain immediate access to all API keys. API keys should be treated as sensitive credentials and stored as hashes (similar to passwords), with the plaintext only displayed once upon creation.

The Webhook model stores webhook secrets in plaintext in the database (field: secret = models.CharField(max_length=64)). Webhook secrets are used to verify the authenticity of webhook payloads, and storing them in plaintext exposes them if the database is compromised.

The course_spool_slot_094 endpoint saves files using user-controlled filenames from either the uploaded file name or the 'packet_ref' GET parameter. While FileSystemStorage may sanitize some characters, path traversal sequences could potentially bypass checks depending on the Django version and platform.

The admin_import endpoint allows bulk user and enrollment creation from CSV files without rate limiting. While it requires admin authentication, it could be abused by administrators or compromised admin accounts to rapidly create resources.
The file_upload endpoint allows authenticated users to upload files without rate limiting. This could be abused to fill storage with large numbers of files or very large files.
The course_frame_slip_671 function explicitly disables XSS protection (X-XSS-Protection: 0) and clears Content-Security-Policy headers, reducing the browser's security protections.

User-controlled username is passed directly to log_action without sanitization. If the username contains special characters or newlines, it could tamper with audit log integrity or inject misleading log entries.
The assignment title (user-controlled) is passed to log_action without sanitization, allowing potential audit log tampering through specially crafted titles containing newlines or special characters.
The assignment title (user-controlled) is passed directly to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection attacks.
The assignment title is passed to log_action without sanitization, allowing potential audit log tampering.
The student's username is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection through malicious usernames.
The student's username from the submission is passed to log_action without sanitization, allowing potential log injection.
The discussion thread title (user-controlled) is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection.
The action parameter from the URL is passed to log_action without sanitization, allowing potential log injection through the action path parameter.
User role information is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection if role names contain special characters.
The course title (user-controlled) is passed to log_action without sanitization, allowing potential log injection.
The cohort name (user-controlled) is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection.
The student's username is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection.
The file title from POST data is passed directly to log_action without sanitization, allowing potential log injection through specially crafted titles.
The resource title is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection.
The student's username is passed to log_action without sanitization, potentially allowing log injection.
The MongoClient connection string does not include TLS/SSL parameters, and the default 'mongodb://localhost:27017' uses unencrypted connections.
The media files are served via Django's static() helper when DEBUG is True. If DEBUG is accidentally enabled in production, this exposes uploaded files directly.

The login is handled by Django's built-in LoginView. Django's auth framework does call `request.session.cycle_key()` after login by default in `django.contrib.auth.login()`, so this is actually handled. However, the signup view at core/views.py (referenced but not shown in this chunk) may authenticate users without session regeneration. Since we only see the URL config pointing to the built-in LoginView, Django handles session regeneration internally.

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are set to `not DEBUG`. If DEBUG is accidentally enabled in production (or the environment variable is misconfigured), cookies will be sent over insecure HTTP connections.
